## Role of this chapter

- Institutional background (Colombian corporate tax system, 1980s) and data description that every later chapter leans on, so it isn't repeated in ch. 4-8.
- Two things downstream chapters cite directly: the juridical-organization split (corps = truth-reporters, used from @sec-testing onward) and the ST-liable/exempt industry split (used in @sec-fiscal).

## Data source {#sec-setting-data}

- Colombian Annual Survey of Manufacturing (EAM), 1981-1991, manufacturing firms with more than 10 employees.
- Firm-level panel: output, intermediates, capital, labour, juridical organization, sales taxes.
- **Timing: the year in the panel is the activity (reference) year.** DANE runs the EAM each year with the economic year immediately preceding collection as the reference period [@DANE1995, p. 40]: the survey for year $x$ is collected during $x+1$ and labelled $x$ (e.g. the 1992–1994 surveys were collected in 1993–1995, and the 1992 file values assets at December 1992; @DANE2018). The observed sales-tax rates confirm this for the 1981–1991 panel: each statutory change shows up in the year the law took effect, not one year later (@tbl-st-by-year, @sec-setting-st).
- UPDATE: state sample size and coverage (industries, years) with the actual filtered N; @tbl-sum-stats gives the working sample after the `is.finite(y,k,l,m)` filter.

![Summary statistics, manufacturing firms in Colombia (1981--1991).](/tables/ch03-summary-stats.png){#tbl-sum-stats}

- Two groups of shares (of revenue): direct cost shares (sales tax, skilled/unskilled labour wages, capital) and the materials/intermediates decomposition (materials, electricity, fuels, repair & maintenance, services, deductible vs. non-deductible intermediates). The materials/deductible split matters later (@sec-testing): only deductible intermediates carry an overreporting incentive.
- Note for the write-up, not a rendering issue: skilled-labour-share SD (1.62) is far above its own mean/Q3 — a small number of extreme outliers in that one column. Decide whether to mention/trim; not addressed in the table itself.

## Juridical organization {#sec-setting-jo}

![Juridical organization, manufacturing firms in Colombia (1981--1991).](/tables/ch03-jo-summary.png){#tbl-jo-summary}

- Five types in the data; four kept in the analysis (Corporation, Limited Liability Company, Partnership, Proprietorship). Others (cooperatives, community/state enterprises) excluded — not profit-driven, no evasion incentive of the kind modelled.
- Definitions (safe to copy from `80-colombia.qmd`, institutional facts, not model output):
  - **Corporation** (*sociedad anónima*): capital association, $N\ge5$ shareholders, tradable shares, liability limited to capital, supervised by the Superintendent of Corporations with a mandatory auditor.
  - **Limited liability company** (*sociedad de responsabilidad limitada*): $2\le N\le20$ (25 in the 1992 EAM documentation), non-tradable shares, liability limited to capital.
  - **Partnership** (*sociedad colectiva* and variants): $N\ge2$, full/joint liability, not a capital association.
  - **Proprietorship**: single individual, full liability.
- Income tax by type: Corporations 40% on distributed dividends; Partnerships and LLCs 20% on profits (whether distributed or not); Proprietorships on the graduated individual schedule (56 brackets, 0.5%-51%).
- Since 1974, a minimum presumptive income (8% of net wealth) applied to individuals and juridical organizations except LLCs. Some industries/regions had the income tax exempted or reduced (airlines, publishing, reforestation; "frontier" regions).

:::{.callout-note}
Institutional summary table (rates/liability/capital/owners by type) — kept as a plain markdown table, not a generated PNG, since it states fixed institutional facts rather than computed statistics:

| Organization | Income tax | Liability | Capital | Owners |
|:--:|:----:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Corporation | 40% (on distributed dividends) | Limited to capital participation | Tradable capital shares | $N\ge5$ |
| Limited Co. | 20% (on profits) | Limited to capital participation | Non-tradable capital shares | $2\le N \le 20\ (25)$ |
| Partnership | 20% (on profits) | Full | Not a capital association | $N\ge2$ |
| Proprietorship | Individual Income Tax | Full | Owner | $N=1$ |
:::

## Sales tax {#sec-setting-st}

- Targeted manufacturing (finished goods, imports). Since 1974, credit for tax paid on purchases (except capital goods) — a VAT in substance.
- Basic rate 15%; preferential 6% for clothing, footwear, popular-housing inputs; 35% on luxury goods. Exports, foodstuffs, drugs, textbooks excluded from the start, along with capital/agricultural inputs and transport/agricultural equipment.
- This is the rate the 1983 reform changed (@sec-fiscal): most ST-liable industries moved from 6% to 10%; ST-exempt industries stayed exempt. State this here as background; the reform and its effect on evasion belong to @sec-fiscal, not here.
- **The 1983 reform: debate, enactment, and effective date.**
  - *Debate (1981–1983).* The Bird–Wiesner Mission (1978–1981), a technical mission on Colombia's intergovernmental finances led by Richard Bird and Eduardo Wiesner, reported in 1981 [@JunguitoRincon2004]. Among its recommendations: better tax administration to reduce evasion, stronger collection tools, wider withholding, and more auditing; the 1983 reforms followed [@Bolanos2019].
  - *Enactment (end of 1983).* Using the extraordinary powers of art. 53 of Ley 9 de 1983, the government issued Decreto 3541 on 29 December 1983 (Diario Oficial No. 36.452, 18 January 1984). It set the general sales-tax rate at 10% (art. 6) and extended the tax to the retail level as a value-added tax [@Decreto3541_1983; @Perry1990].
  - *Effective date (1 April 1984).* The pre-reform sales tax applied until 31 March 1984; the value-added tax applied from 1 April 1984 (art. 92 of Decreto 3541) [@CorteConstitucional2016]. @Perry1990 likewise date the new structure to "the reforms of April 1984". So **1983 is the last full pre-reform year and 1984 is a partial year**.
  - *1990 reform.* Ley 49 de 1990 (28 December 1990) raised the general rate to 12% from 1 January 1991 (art. 26) [@Ley49_1990].
- **The 1983 reform also cut income-tax rates** [@PerryCardenas1986, vol. 1, p. 36; @Ocampo1983]. Ley 9 de 1983 lowered the individual schedule, and thus the rates faced by Proprietorships, to offset the rise in effective rates caused by inflation since 1974 (bracket creep); the new schedule still left real incidence about 8% above 1974 in most brackets. Relative to the 1982 schedule, average rates fell by 4.6 percentage points on average across brackets, or 10–35% of the 1982 rates above the lowest bracket (@tbl-inc-tax-1983). The top individual rate fell from 56% to 49%. LLCs' rate fell from 20% to 18%, to compensate them for being brought under the presumptive income regime by the same law.

:::{#tbl-inc-tax-1983}
![](/tables/ch03-income-tax-1983.png)

Average individual income-tax rates by taxable income, 1982 schedule (Decreto 2809) vs. the 1983 schedule that stayed (Decreto 397, Ley 9 de 1983), transcribed from Perry and Cárdenas (1986), Cuadro III.1.
:::

- **Marginal rates fell less than average rates at both ends of the distribution** (@tbl-marg-tax-1983). The incentive to overreport costs depends on the marginal rate, but Ley 9 de 1983 presented its schedule in average rates, which @PerryCardenas1986 [p. 36] call "simple cosmética política". Implied marginal rates, computed from the average rates in @tbl-inc-tax-1983, fell by up to 12.7 percentage points in the middle of the distribution, but barely changed at low incomes (+0.5 percentage points between 200,000 and 300,000 pesos) and fell only about 2 percentage points above 1,000,000 pesos.

:::{#tbl-marg-tax-1983}
![](/tables/ch03-marginal-tax-1983.png)

Implied marginal income-tax rates by income interval, 1982 vs. 1983 schedules, computed from the average rates in @tbl-inc-tax-1983 as the change in tax over the change in income between consecutive points. Each figure is an average over the interval.
:::
- **The observed rates match the reforms' timing** (@tbl-st-by-year). The median rate paid on sales is 6% in 1981–1983, 10% from 1985, and 12% in 1991. In 1984 it is 9%, exactly what three months at 6% and nine months at 10% give ($0.25\times6\%+0.75\times10\%=9\%$).

:::{#tbl-st-by-year}
![](/tables/ch03-st-by-year.png)

Observed sales-tax rate on sales by survey year, against the statutory general rate in force. Rows in bold are the years a reform took effect: 1984 (Decreto 3541 de 1983, from 1 April) and 1991 (Ley 49 de 1990, from 1 January). Firms with a rate strictly between 0 and 50%.
:::

## Why corporations are the least likely evaders {#sec-setting-corp-evasion}

- Three institutional reasons (from `80-colombia.qmd`'s discussion), each mapped to a modelling choice:
  1. Mandatory auditor and Superintendent oversight $\to$ higher detection probability $q$ for corps in the model.
  2. Tradable shares create a market-value cost to underreporting profits $\to$ an implicit cost channel outside $\kappa(e,\omega)$, not separately modelled.
  3. The income tax on distributed (not accrued) dividends gives corporations a timing margin ordinary profit-shifting doesn't have.
- This is the institutional justification for treating corps as $e=0$ in stage 1 (@sec-testing, @sec-deconvolution) — state it here once, reference it there.
- Proprietorships, partnerships and LLCs face both income-tax and ST incentives to overreport; incentives vary by industry (ST rate) and by juridical organization within industry (income-tax rate) — sets up @sec-fiscal's identification strategy.
